cards.meaning: An action or comment that is deliberately cruel, unfair, or disloyal.
cards.nuance: It suggests an attack on someone’s dignity, efforts, or reputation rather than an ordinary criticism. Often used when the attack feels personal or underhanded.
cards.literal: A punch aimed below the waist in boxing.

uses.where: Team meeting · criticism of a colleague
uses.sentence: Calling me incompetent was a low blow, especially when I had stayed late to finish the report.
uses.tip: Use it for comments that seem needlessly personal or disloyal.

uses.sentence: Making fun of her accent after she introduced me was a real low blow.
uses.tip: Often intensified with ‘real’ or ‘pretty’.

uses.sentence: The review was a low blow, belittling the artist’s background instead of discussing the exhibition.
uses.tip: Useful in opinion writing when describing a deliberately derogatory attack.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from boxing, where a low blow is a punch below the waist. It was later used figuratively for a cruel or disloyal action.

timeline.text: Boxing and newspapers use the literal expression for a punch or blow aimed below the waist.
Writers begin applying it to unfair remarks and harmful actions.
It describes a personal attack delivered in a mean or underhanded way.

cards.pitfall: Usually used as a noun, often in the form ‘a low blow’; it is not normally a verb.

cards.meaning: To show that you are serious and ready to take firm action.
cards.nuance: It signals determination, often with an implied warning or threat. Use it when someone wants others to know they will not tolerate delays, excuses, or poor performance.
cards.literal: Treating something as a serious purpose rather than a casual matter.

uses.sentence: The director means business about improving the team’s delivery rate.
uses.tip: Often used to signal that a warning is serious.

uses.sentence: If he keeps insulting people, I’m going to mean business.
uses.tip: Works when someone is about to set a firm boundary.

uses.sentence: The new policy makes clear that the company means business about data protection.
uses.tip: Common in formal reports, statements, and workplace messages.

origin.summary: The phrase probably grew from older expressions about getting down to serious business. It was in use by the 19th century, when it could mean acting with purpose, and later developed the stronger sense of being ready to enforce rules.

timeline.text: The phrase appears in writing, initially suggesting serious purpose or determined action.
It becomes associated with firmness, warnings, and enforcing discipline.
It is used to show that someone is serious about a situation.

cards.pitfall: Use it when describing determination, not as a synonym for being busy. “I have a lot of work to do” does not necessarily mean business.

cards.meaning: To be the person experiencing criticism, blame, or an unwanted consequence.
cards.nuance: It often suggests that the other person is actively delivering criticism, blame, or bad news. It can sound formal in workplace writing but is natural in conversation.
cards.literal: Being at the end of a line where blows, messages, or other unwanted things arrive.

uses.sentence: After missing two deadlines, she was on the receiving end of some tough feedback.
uses.tip: Common when describing criticism or blame directed at someone.

uses.sentence: I suggested cancelling the trip, so I was on the receiving end of my friends’ complaints.
uses.tip: Often follows an action that affects other people.

uses.where: News report · reaction to a policy
uses.sentence: Small businesses were on the receiving end of complaints about the new fees.
uses.tip: Useful for reporting who is experiencing criticism or harm.

origin.summary: The phrase probably developed from the idea of being positioned to receive blows or messages. Its figurative use for experiencing criticism was established by the early 20th century.

timeline.text: The expression appears in contexts involving someone being at the end of a line and receiving blows or communications.
Its use broadened to mean experiencing blame, criticism, or other unwelcome effects.
It commonly identifies the person facing negative feedback or consequences.

cards.pitfall: It describes the person receiving criticism or an unwanted effect, not the person delivering it.

cards.meaning: To criticize or attack someone forcefully, or to eat something quickly and eagerly.
cards.nuance: The meaning depends on context: use it for fierce criticism or vigorous action, including starting to eat with great enthusiasm.
cards.literal: Tearing something apart with force, especially food or an opponent.

uses.sentence: The director rip into the proposal and challenged every major assumption.
uses.tip: Often describes forceful criticism of a person, plan, or performance.

uses.sentence: The children rip into the pizza before anyone had finished serving the drinks.
uses.tip: With food, it means eating quickly and eagerly.

uses.sentence: The columnist rips into the policy in a sharp, well-argued article.
uses.tip: Common in forceful editorial writing about people, organizations, or decisions.

origin.summary: The exact origin is unclear. The phrase probably grew from older senses of “rip,” meaning to tear apart or attack forcefully, combined with “into” to emphasize vigorous action.

timeline.text: “Rip” was used for pulling something apart and for attacking with force.
Writers began using “rip into” for fierce criticism or vigorous physical action.
It can describe forceful criticism or eating food eagerly.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with “rip off,” which means to steal from or unfairly overcharge someone.

cards.hint: blame the person bringing bad news
cards.meaning: To blame or punish someone for delivering unwelcome news instead of dealing with the problem itself.
cards.nuance: It criticizes an unfair reaction to bad news. Use it when someone focuses on blaming the reporter rather than fixing the issue.
cards.literal: Attacking the person who brings a message.

uses.sentence: The client wanted to shoot the messenger, but the team needed to discuss why the deadline was missed.
uses.tip: Often follows ‘tried to’ or ‘wanted to’ when describing an unreasonable response.

uses.sentence: My friend changed the plan, and I joked that I was about to shoot the messenger.
uses.tip: Usually humorous or lightly accusing, rather than a serious threat.

uses.sentence: Managers should support teams receiving criticism, not shoot the messenger who reports it.
uses.tip: Useful in writing about accountability, feedback, and transparent communication.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from the idea that a person bringing bad news may be blamed or harmed for the message rather than for causing the problem. Its exact earliest origin is uncertain.

timeline.text: Stories and sayings warned that people might punish or attack those who brought unwelcome news.
The idea appears in English writing, including a reference to killing or attacking a messenger who delivers bad news.
Means blaming the person who reports a problem instead of addressing the problem itself.

cards.pitfall: It means blaming the news-bearer; it does not mean to reject the news itself.

cards.meaning: To avoid taking a clear position in an argument or decision.
cards.nuance: It often suggests deliberate caution or indecision. It can describe someone waiting for more information, but it can also criticise them for refusing to commit.
cards.literal: Someone sitting on top of a fence without stepping down to either side.

uses.sentence: We need a decision by Friday; sitting on the fence will delay the project.
uses.tip: Useful when someone is deliberately avoiding responsibility for a choice.

uses.sentence: You’re sitting on the fence about dinner, so just choose the Italian place.
uses.tip: Often used teasingly when someone cannot make even a minor decision.

uses.sentence: Several members continued to sit on the fence when the committee voted on the proposal.
uses.tip: Common in reporting about politics, negotiations and divided groups.

origin.summary: The image comes from choosing between two sides, especially political ones. The phrase was in use by the early 1800s and later became a general expression for refusing to commit.

timeline.text: The phrase appears in writing as a metaphor for maintaining a neutral position between opposing sides.
Its use expands beyond politics to describe neutrality in arguments, decisions and negotiations.
It can be neutral, describing caution, or critical, implying wishy-washiness.

cards.pitfall: Sitting on the fence is not simply waiting; it usually implies avoiding a clear position even when a choice is expected.

cards.meaning: Clear, convincing evidence that proves something happened.
cards.nuance: It suggests the evidence is so direct that the explanation is hard to dispute. It is common in investigations, workplaces and everyday arguments.
cards.literal: A gun that has just been fired, leaving obvious smoke behind.

uses.sentence: The duplicate receipts were the smoking gun that proved he had claimed the same costs twice.
uses.tip: Use it for evidence that settles a question rather than merely supporting a suspicion.

uses.sentence: Her handprint on the vase was the smoking gun, so nobody else needed to guess who dropped it.
uses.tip: Often used when someone is caught out and the proof is obvious.

uses.sentence: The timestamped recording became the smoking gun in the case against the fraudster.
uses.tip: Effective in reporting when evidence provides a decisive link.

origin.summary: The phrase appeared in 19th-century writing, but its exact origin is unclear. It likely refers literally to a recently fired gun and figuratively to evidence that leaves no room for doubt.

timeline.text: Early English uses connect a smoking gun with something obvious or unmistakable.
The expression becomes established for clear proof in investigations and arguments.
Means decisive evidence that directly supports a conclusion.

cards.pitfall: It does not mean merely a strong clue; the evidence should be compelling and hard to dispute.

cards.meaning: To deceive someone or treat them badly, often for your own advantage.
cards.nuance: It suggests a false promise, betrayal, or exploitation. The phrase often appears in accusations and is especially common in American English.
cards.literal: Giving someone a ride in a vehicle.

uses.sentence: I think the supplier took us for a ride with those exaggerated delivery estimates.
uses.tip: Use it when someone has knowingly misled you.

uses.sentence: He claimed he could fix my laptop for free, but I think he was just taking me for a ride.
uses.tip: Often sounds like a warning that a deal is dishonest.

uses.sentence: Several customers said the online shop took them for a ride with fake discount claims.
uses.tip: A blunt option for reporting deliberate deception in informal writing.

origin.summary: The idiom probably grew from the literal idea of taking someone along for a ride, then extended to carrying them away under false pretenses. Its exact development is not clearly documented.

timeline.text: People used the literal expression of giving someone a ride in a vehicle.
The expression began appearing in senses connected with deception and mistreatment.
It usually means deceiving or exploiting someone.

similar: pull the wool over someone’s eyes
cards.pitfall: When no deception is involved, say ‘take someone for a ride’ only if you mean a literal outing.

cards.term: take matters into one's own hands
cards.meaning: To deal with a problem yourself instead of relying on someone else to handle it.
cards.nuance: It suggests direct action and personal responsibility. It can sound determined, but it may also imply that someone has stopped waiting for an official process.
cards.literal: Taking a problem into your own hands so that you can control what happens.

uses.where: Team stand-up · fixing a delayed launch
uses.sentence: After waiting weeks for approval, we took matters into our own hands and fixed the release process.
uses.highlight: took matters into our own hands
uses.tip: Common when a team decides it cannot depend on another group.

uses.sentence: The residents took matters into their own hands and repaired the gate themselves.
uses.highlight: took matters into their own hands
uses.tip: Often implies bypassing delay, rules or outside help.

uses.sentence: Volunteers took matters into their own hands after months of unanswered complaints.
uses.highlight: took matters into their own hands
uses.tip: Useful in reporting when a group acts without waiting for authorities.

origin.summary: The wording dates back to the early modern period, when taking something physically into one's hand meant handling it personally. The modern figurative sense developed from that literal idea of direct control.

timeline.text: Early uses refer to handling or managing something personally.
The phrase comes to mean dealing with a problem directly rather than leaving it to others.
It describes taking personal control of a situation, often after delay or frustration.

similar: take things into your own hands
cards.pitfall: Usually the phrase is plural: “take matters into your own hands,” “take matters into their own hands.”

cards.meaning: To keep asking or trying after someone has already said no.
cards.nuance: It often suggests stubborn persistence and can feel frustrated, persuasive or even pushy, depending on the context.
cards.literal: Treat someone’s “no” as if it were something other than an answer.

uses.sentence: The team wouldn’t take no for an answer, so they offered to split the work.
uses.highlight: wouldn’t take no for an answer
uses.tip: Shows persistence, but avoid making the request sound demanding.

uses.sentence: He wouldn’t take no for an answer and kept asking me to borrow my car.
uses.highlight: wouldn’t take no for an answer
uses.tip: Common when describing someone who keeps pursuing a request.

uses.sentence: Determined to improve the offer, the sales team refused to take no for an answer.
uses.highlight: refused to take no for an answer
uses.tip: Useful in reporting how someone pursued negotiations.

origin.summary: The phrase is recorded from the early 1800s and uses the idea that a person treats “no” as an answer they can continue to challenge.

timeline.text: The expression first appears in English writing in the form “take no for an answer.”
Its use becomes established for persistent or repeated attempts to get a different response.
It describes refusing to give up after being rejected.

similar: not take no for an answer
cards.pitfall: The expression normally takes a form such as “she wouldn’t take no for an answer”; don’t use it when someone is simply ignoring a refusal.

cards.term: take the wind out of someone's sails
cards.meaning: To make someone lose confidence, enthusiasm, or momentum.
cards.nuance: It describes reducing someone’s strength or willingness to act, often through bad news or criticism. It can sound blunt, so use it carefully when the person may be sensitive.
cards.literal: Removing the wind from a ship’s sails so the ship cannot move forward.

uses.sentence: The sudden budget cuts took the wind out of our sails.
uses.highlight: took the wind out of our sails
uses.tip: Often describes a setback that weakens motivation or momentum.

uses.sentence: Her unexpected cancellation took the wind out of my sails.
uses.highlight: took the wind out of my sails
uses.tip: Natural when one event spoils your excitement or plans.

uses.sentence: The delay took the wind out of the team’s sails, and productivity fell sharply.
uses.highlight: took the wind out of the team’s sails
uses.tip: Useful in reporting when explaining a loss of confidence or momentum.

origin.summary: The expression comes from sailing. If the wind is removed from a ship’s sails, the ship loses its power to move, just as a person may lose confidence or enthusiasm.

timeline.text: Sailors used the movement of the wind and sails as a familiar image for controlling a ship’s speed and direction.
Writers began using the idea of taking the wind from sails figuratively.
It means weakening someone’s confidence, enthusiasm, or ability to make progress.

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse it with ‘steal someone’s thunder’, which means taking attention or credit from someone else.

cards.meaning: The less harmful option when neither choice is good.
cards.nuance: It acknowledges an unwelcome choice but emphasizes that one option has fewer drawbacks. Use it when comparing bad alternatives, often to justify a practical decision.
cards.literal: One of two harmful things is smaller or less serious than the other.

uses.sentence: Delaying the launch is the lesser of two evils compared with releasing a broken product.
uses.tip: Useful for weighing two imperfect business options.

uses.sentence: Hiring a small band was the lesser of two evils because a DJ was too expensive.
uses.tip: Often sounds practical, slightly resigned, and informal.

uses.sentence: Some criticism may be the lesser of two evils if it prevents a more serious problem.
uses.tip: Common in measured arguments and professional writing.

origin.summary: The expression comes from the old philosophical idea that, when faced with two evils, people should choose the less harmful one. Its earliest exact wording is difficult to trace, but the concept appears in ancient Greek and Roman thought.

timeline.text: Philosophers discussed choosing the lesser evil when both available choices were harmful.
Early English uses of ‘lesser evil’ reflect that older philosophical comparison.
The phrase names the less harmful option between two undesirable choices.

similar: damned if we do, damned if we don’t
cards.pitfall: It does not mean the choice is good—only that it is less bad than the alternative.

cards.meaning: To admit defeat and stop trying to win or succeed.
cards.nuance: It means giving up after effort has failed, often with resignation rather than a strategic retreat. It can describe one person, a team, or an organization.
cards.literal: In boxing, a defeated fighter’s seconds signal surrender by throwing a towel into the ring.

uses.sentence: We may have to throw in the towel and postpone the product launch until next quarter.
uses.tip: Often followed by a practical alternative or next step.

uses.sentence: I’m throwing in the towel before the rest of you realize how good you are.
uses.tip: Can sound playful when the defeat is harmless.

uses.sentence: The champion threw in the towel after the third round, ending a determined but unsuccessful defence.
uses.tip: Common in reports about matches, races, and other contests.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from boxing, where a fighter’s seconds could signal surrender by throwing a towel into the ring. An earlier expression used a sponge instead of a towel.

timeline.text: Boxing reports describe the expression “throw up the sponge,” referring to ending a fight.
The form with “towel” appears in English writing and becomes the familiar expression.
It means admitting defeat and abandoning a contest or effort.

cards.pitfall: It means accepting defeat, not simply taking a short break or changing strategy.

cards.meaning: To expose someone to blame, danger, or harsh consequences in order to protect yourself or others.
cards.nuance: It suggests abandoning someone or making them take the full force of a problem. It can sound deliberately cold or accusatory, so use it carefully in professional settings.
cards.literal: Giving a person to wolves to be attacked.

uses.where: Team meeting · explaining a failed project
uses.sentence: The director threw the contractor to the wolves when the budget was questioned.
uses.highlight: threw the contractor to the wolves
uses.tip: The object of the phrase can be a person, group, or project.

uses.sentence: Don’t throw your brother to the wolves just because you disagree with him.
uses.highlight: throw your brother to the wolves
uses.tip: Use it when someone is being blamed or left to face trouble alone.

uses.sentence: The company threw the junior team to the wolves while senior leaders avoided scrutiny.
uses.highlight: threw the junior team to the wolves
uses.tip: It is forceful and often implies unfair or strategic blame-shifting.

origin.summary: The phrase likely comes from the older image of throwing prey to wolves. Its figurative use, meaning to sacrifice or expose someone to attack, appears in English by the nineteenth century.

timeline.text: The image of a person or animal being thrown to wolves represents being abandoned to danger or attack.
The figurative expression is recorded in English for sacrificing someone or something to harsh treatment.
It means exposing or abandoning someone so that they bear the blame or consequences.

cards.pitfall: Unlike ‘scapegoat’, which can describe a person blamed for wrongdoing, this phrase often emphasizes the act of exposing or abandoning them.

cards.meaning: A difficult decision between two or more options that each have significant drawbacks.
cards.nuance: It sounds informal but confident, suggesting that the choice is genuinely hard rather than simply inconvenient.
cards.literal: A call that is difficult to make, as when someone must choose between equally demanding options.

uses.sentence: Choosing between delaying the launch and shipping a weaker product was a tough call.
uses.tip: Common when discussing deadlines, trade-offs and business priorities.

uses.sentence: It was a tough call between the quiet Italian place and the lively pub.
uses.tip: Works in relaxed conversation when two options are close in value.

uses.sentence: The team made a tough call to postpone the feature until the underlying issues were fixed.
uses.tip: Often followed by ‘to’ plus the action that was chosen.

origin.summary: The exact origin is uncertain, but the phrase appears to have developed from the idea of making a difficult choice or judgment.

timeline.text: Phrases using ‘call’ for a choice or decision become established in English.
‘Tough call’ gains everyday use for a decision involving competing drawbacks.
Common in work, social conversation and informal writing.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it for an easy decision; ‘tough’ is the key distinction.

cards.hint: a fight over territory or control
cards.meaning: A bitter struggle between rivals competing for control of the same area, market, or area of influence.
cards.nuance: It suggests an ongoing contest in which each side protects its own territory and tries to weaken the other. It is usually more hostile than a simple disagreement.
cards.literal: Rival groups fighting to control the same patch of ground.

uses.sentence: The sales teams are engaged in a turf war over the biggest clients.
uses.tip: Suggests competition for control of customers, accounts, or responsibility.

uses.sentence: Two local groups started a turf war over who could use the community hall.
uses.tip: Often implies an unnecessarily competitive dispute over shared space.

uses.sentence: The article describes a turf war between the two streaming companies.
uses.tip: Useful for describing fierce competition over customers, territory, or influence.

origin.summary: The expression developed from the literal idea of rival groups claiming the same ground. Its early use was often political, before businesses adopted it for commercial competition.

timeline.text: “Turf” was commonly used for a territory or area of control, especially in American political language.
The phrase began appearing in descriptions of fights for local political influence.
It describes any fierce dispute over territory, customers, market share, or authority.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it for every disagreement; it implies a competitive struggle over control.

cards.meaning: To deliberately ignore something bad, inconvenient or wrong that you have noticed.
cards.nuance: It implies awareness and a conscious choice not to act. It is usually critical when describing a person, organisation or government.
cards.literal: Turning one’s eyes away so that something cannot be seen.

uses.sentence: Managers cannot turn a blind eye when employees repeatedly ignore safety rules.
uses.tip: Often used when someone ignores a problem they clearly know about.

uses.sentence: We’ve discussed his drinking for months, but everyone keeps turning a blind eye.
uses.tip: The phrase can refer to a whole group choosing not to acknowledge a problem.

uses.sentence: The regulator has been accused of turning a blind eye to pollution from local factories.
uses.tip: Frequent in reporting and campaigns about official failures to act.

origin.summary: The expression developed from the idea of deliberately looking away from something visible. Its wording is recorded in the early 1800s and may echo older religious language about turning away one’s eyes.

timeline.text: Religious writing already used the idea of turning away one’s eyes to describe refusing to notice or understand.
The exact expression appears in published writing, including a description of turning a blind eye to something.
Means knowingly ignoring a problem or wrongdoing.

cards.pitfall: It describes deliberate ignorance, not simply failing to notice something.

cards.meaning: To reject, refuse, or decline an offer, request, proposal, or opportunity.
cards.nuance: Use it for a clear negative response, especially when an offer, invitation, or job is involved. It can sound polite, but firmer than a simple “no.”

uses.sentence: She turned down the offer because the salary didn’t match her experience.
uses.tip: Common when declining a job, proposal, or business offer.

uses.sentence: We turned down the invitation and stayed in for the evening.
uses.tip: A natural way to decline an invitation or suggestion.

uses.sentence: The committee turned down our request for an earlier deadline.
uses.tip: Often used in formal reports and correspondence.

origin.summary: The phrase developed from the older verb “turn,” which could mean to direct or move something, combined with “down” in the sense of lowering or reversing its direction. Its figurative use for rejection became established during the nineteenth century.

timeline.text: The word “turn” could mean to direct, move, or change the direction of something.
People used “turn down” for lowering, directing, or rejecting something.
The phrase was firmly established in the figurative sense of refusing or declining.

cards.pitfall: When talking about volume or heat, “turn it down” means reduce it, not reject it.

cards.meaning: When more forceful action is needed to deal with a difficult situation.
cards.nuance: It suggests escalating from discussion or gentle pressure to decisive action. Use it when circumstances force you to act rather than continue waiting or avoiding the issue.
cards.literal: A situation in which people begin physically pushing and shoving because ordinary methods have failed.

uses.sentence: When push comes to shove, we’ll postpone the new features and fix the payment bug first.
uses.tip: Use it when discussing how priorities may change under pressure.

uses.sentence: When push comes to shove, we’ll split the bill and book the smaller restaurant.
uses.tip: Often signals a practical fallback after people disagree.

uses.sentence: When push comes to shove, the team can reduce the scope rather than delay the launch.
uses.tip: Common in informal business writing and contingency plans.

origin.summary: The phrase developed from the literal idea of pushing and shoving when stronger physical force is needed. Its figurative use became established during the 1800s.

timeline.text: The words push and shove were commonly used for applying physical force in a crowd or dispute.
The combined phrase appeared in writing for forceful action and later developed its modern figurative meaning.
It means taking firmer action when a situation cannot be resolved by discussion or delay.

cards.pitfall: It describes taking stronger action under pressure; it does not mean someone is physically pushing another person.

cards.meaning: To be stuck with the most undesirable result from each of two alternatives.
cards.nuance: It describes a situation in which every option has serious drawbacks, so choosing one still leaves a problem.
cards.literal: The worst possible outcome from each of two choices.

uses.where: Job offer · deciding whether to relocate
uses.sentence: Taking the promotion means losing weekends, while staying means missing the raise.
uses.highlight: Taking the promotion means losing weekends
uses.tip: Use it when both available choices have clear drawbacks.

uses.sentence: The cheap place has terrible reviews, and the expensive one is fully booked—the worst of both worlds.
uses.tip: Natural when describing two disappointing alternatives.

uses.where: Housing market · reporting on a new rule
uses.sentence: Smaller landlords may face the worst of both worlds as costs rise while demand falls.
uses.tip: Common in reports about difficult conditions or competing pressures.

origin.summary: The exact origin is unclear. The expression appears to have developed from the older idea of having the “best of both worlds,” but its negative form is not tied to a documented first use.

timeline.text: The expression “best of both worlds” is used for combining advantages from two different situations.
The negative form “worst of both worlds” becomes established for situations combining two disadvantages.
It refers broadly to the least favorable result from each of two alternatives.

similar: caught between a rock and a hard place
cards.pitfall: It describes unfavorable alternatives, not simply something that is very bad.
